title: Risk-Based Inspection in Canada: ABSA, TSSA and CSA B51
description: How risk-based inspection works under Canada's provincial pressure equipment regulators, and how Atlantis delivers remote RBI studies for Canadian plants.
h1: Risk-based inspection for Canadian refineries, upgraders and storage terminals
intro: Canadian integrity managers work under a patchwork: pressure equipment is regulated province by province, atmospheric tanks sit outside those laws altogether, and pipeline terminals answer to a federal regulator. This page explains what ABSA in Alberta, TSSA in Ontario and the other provincial authorities expect when an owner moves equipment onto risk-based intervals, where Canada's refining and tank storage is concentrated, and how Atlantis runs an RBI study remotely for a Canadian site, from the first data request to an inspection plan your in-service inspector can sign off.

highlights.p: In Canada the legal requirement comes from the provincial act and its regulation, with CSA B51 governing design registration. API RP 580 and 581 supply the method, but the province decides how far an owner may rely on it for equipment the regulator oversees.

highlights.h: Built to sit inside your system
highlights.p: An RBI study is most useful when it plugs into the owner-user integrity management system the regulator already audits. We structure the register, plans and change triggers so they can be adopted as procedures in that system, not filed beside it.

Workshops are held in the plant's own hours, whether that is Mountain time in Edmonton and Hardisty, Eastern time in Sarnia or Atlantic time in Saint John. Document review continues between sessions, and no travel is needed for the study itself.

sections.h: How pressure equipment and tanks are regulated in Canada
p: Canada has no single national pressure equipment law. Each province and territory has its own act and regulation, a regulator or delegated authority to administer it, and its own rules for in-service inspection. CSA B51, the boiler, pressure vessel and pressure piping code, is adopted across the country for design registration, but what happens to a vessel once it is in service depends on where it sits.

Atmospheric storage tanks are not pressure equipment, so the provincial pressure equipment regime does not reach them. Their integrity programmes rest on fire codes, environmental approvals and industry practice, which in refining and terminals usually means API 653. Tanks and facilities that belong to an interprovincial or international pipeline are a separate case again: they are managed inside the pipeline company's management system under the Canada Energy Regulator's Onshore Pipeline Regulations, which also call for an integrity management programme.

The table summarises the regimes an RBI study for a Canadian site most often has to respect. Where a regulator has not published a position on risk-based intervals, we say so and recommend confirming the approach before the plan is adopted.

p: Alberta's approach is performance-based. ABSA does not inspect most refinery and upgrader equipment itself; instead it accepts and audits the owner-user's pressure equipment integrity management system, and in-service inspections are certified by in-service pressure equipment inspectors certified under AB-526, employed by the owner-user or by an integrity assessment organisation that ABSA recognises. Maximum inspection and servicing intervals are set out in AB-506.

ABSA has treated risk-based inspection as something an owner-user may adopt within that system, provided the programme meets ABSA's requirements and is covered by the owner-user audit. Its original RBI requirements, issued in 2001, asked for an accurate equipment inventory with design data, a logical and fully documented process, management of change and risk policies set by senior management, and said that contracting RBI work to an outside firm needed ABSA review case by case. ABSA's current RBI requirements are published as AB-505, the document the Alberta supplement to AB-512H refers to. Check the current position with ABSA before an outside study starts; the owner-user remains accountable for the programme whoever carries out the analysis.

Atlantis is not an ABSA integrity assessment organisation and does not certify inspections. Our role in Alberta is the engineering analysis behind the plan: corrosion loops, damage mechanisms, probability and consequence, and the inspection tasks that follow, documented so the in-service inspector and an ABSA auditor can trace each decision.

sections.h: Ontario: TSSA certificates and owner-user self-inspection
p: In Ontario the legal test is simple to state: regulated boilers and pressure vessels need a current Certificate of Inspection under Ontario Regulation 220/01, based on periodic inspection by TSSA or, for insured equipment, by the insurer's inspector. Large plants can instead hold a TSSA certificate for owner-user self-inspection. TSSA's guideline for that certificate expects a plant in continuous operation, two or more qualified and certified inspectors with no production responsibility, annual internal audits of the quality programme and, in the petrochemical industry, inspectors holding API 510 and 570 certificates. Certificates of Authorization run for three years and TSSA may audit the programme annually.

That guideline is silent on risk-based intervals. In practice Sarnia and Nanticoke refiners run API-based inspection programmes on top of the legal minimum, and RBI shapes the scope and timing of inspection within the cycle the certificate requires. An RBI plan for Ontario equipment should therefore flag any item where the proposed due date would fall outside the periodic inspection the certificate depends on, so the owner can resolve it with TSSA rather than discover the conflict at renewal.

sections.h: Storage tanks: outside pressure equipment law, inside API 653
p: For tank farms the controlling document is normally the owner's own API 653 programme. The standard's alternative internal inspection interval, which relies on an RBI assessment carried out to API RP 580, is the usual route to risk-based tank intervals, and in most provinces no pressure equipment regulator stands between the owner and that decision. Fire codes, environmental approvals and insurers still expect a documented, defensible programme, and terminal tanks owned by a federally regulated pipeline must fit the company's CER management system.

Canadian tank RBI has its own emphases. Hardisty and Edmonton tank farms hold heavy and diluted crudes whose water and sediment drive bottom-side and product-side floor corrosion; winter cold changes how roofs, seals and drains behave; and frost and freeze-thaw cycles affect foundations and the annular area. Saint John adds a marine atmosphere and refinery product tankage. Each of those conditions changes the probability side of the assessment, and each needs data the study asks for by name.

sections.h: Where Canada's refining and tank storage is concentrated
p: Four places carry most of the refining, upgrading and tank storage that RBI programmes in Canada are built around. Edmonton and Alberta's Industrial Heartland hold the Suncor Edmonton and Imperial Strathcona refineries, the Sturgeon refinery, the Scotford refining, chemicals and upgrading complex, and NGL fractionation and storage around Fort Saskatchewan. Hardisty, east of Edmonton, is a crude oil storage and terminal hub where large tank farms feed export pipelines. Sarnia's Chemical Valley on the St. Clair River combines Imperial's and Suncor's Sarnia refineries with NOVA Chemicals' ethylene and polyethylene operations. Saint John in New Brunswick is home to the Irving Oil refinery, the largest in Canada, beside the Saint John LNG terminal, known as Canaport LNG until 2021, and a deep-water port.
Each hub page goes into the facilities, the damage mechanisms that tend to drive risk there and the rules that apply.

sections.h: What Canadian owners usually need from an outside RBI study
p: The Canadian requests we expect to see are shaped by the integrity management model and by the crude slate. A study is scoped differently depending on which of these applies.
list: Reviewing an RBI programme ahead of an owner-user audit, so every interval, assumption and change trigger can be traced in the way the regulator expects
Extending an existing RBI programme to equipment that came with an acquisition or a debottleneck and was never assessed under the owner's methodology
Reassessing units after a change in crude slate, for example more heavy, high-acid or diluted crude, which can move naphthenic acid and sulfidation risk sharply
Ranking a large tank farm so out-of-service inspections and floor scans go first to the tanks whose condition and consequence justify it
Building a cold-climate CUI programme in which insulation type, operating temperature cycles and jacketing condition drive inspection priority
Translating a qualitative screening into a semi-quantitative or API RP 581 quantitative assessment for the units where the finer ranking changes decisions

sections.h: Running the study remotely across Canadian time zones
p: Everything starts in a shared data room. We ask for P&IDs and PFDs, heat and material balances, equipment datasheets and manufacturer's data reports or registration records, the inspection and thickness history, process chemistry and the integrity operating windows the plant runs to. Before workshops are booked, the data is screened and a gap log is issued so the plant knows early which missing items will force conservative assumptions.

Corrosion loops and damage mechanisms are assigned to API 571 and challenged in video workshops with your process, operations, corrosion and inspection specialists, scheduled in the plant's own hours. Probability and consequence follow the level the scope calls for: qualitative screening, semi-quantitative ranking, a quantitative assessment to API RP 581, or your corporate RBI standard. The output is a plan per item, with method, coverage, expected effectiveness and a due date, plus CML and TML optimisation where the history supports it. Atlantis works from offices in Houston and Hyderabad, so the study team overlaps Canadian working days for meetings and continues document review outside them.

The study does not require anyone from Atlantis on site. Walkdowns and data verification in Canada are carried out by your own inspectors or your inspection contractor. Where a gap matters, the report names the measurement needed, the method and the coverage, so your contractor can collect it and the model can be updated.

sections.h: Inspection data quality and personnel schemes
p: RBI credits past inspection only as far as that inspection was effective, so the study asks who took the readings, to which procedure and with what coverage. Many Canadian owners and CSA-based projects require NDT personnel certified to CAN/CGSB-48.9712, the Canadian adoption of ISO 9712, through Natural Resources Canada's certification body or CWB Group, and AB-512H expects validated NDE procedures and verified personnel qualification. Recording that information beside each inspection lets the assessment credit good data properly and give less weight to data whose basis cannot be shown.

sections.h: Who signs the plan in Canada
p: The RBI deliverable is a recommendation with its reasoning. Acceptance belongs to the people the provincial system recognises: in Alberta the in-service pressure equipment inspector working within the owner-user's accepted system, in Ontario the TSSA inspector, the insurer's inspector or the owner-user's certified self-inspection staff, and elsewhere the authority the province names. Atlantis does not act as inspector of record and does not certify inspections in any province.

If inspection under the new plan finds damage that needs an engineering assessment of continued operation, the fitness-for-service work stays with the owner's engineer, and Atlantis does not carry out API 579-1 assessments. Once that assessment is made, the RBI model is updated with the outcome.

faqs.a: ABSA has published requirements for RBI programmes since 2001, currently in AB-505, and an owner-user can adopt RBI within its accepted pressure equipment integrity management system, with the RBI programme covered by ABSA's audit. In-service inspections are still certified by inspectors recognised under ABSA's requirements, and AB-506 sets the inspection and servicing requirements the programme works alongside. Confirm the current details with ABSA before relying on extended intervals.

faqs.q: Can an outside firm carry out the RBI study for an Alberta owner-user?
faqs.a: The analysis can be done by an outside firm, but the owner-user stays accountable for the programme. ABSA's original RBI requirements said contracted RBI work needed case-by-case review by ABSA, so check the current expectation before the study starts. We document every input and decision so the owner-user can adopt the results inside its own system.

faqs.q: Does TSSA allow risk-based intervals in Ontario?
faqs.a: TSSA's guideline for owner-user self-inspection does not address risk-based intervals, and regulated equipment still needs a current Certificate of Inspection under O. Reg. 220/01. Refiners use RBI to shape scope and timing within that cycle. Our plans flag any item where the proposed due date would conflict with the certificate, so you can settle it with TSSA in advance.

faqs.q: Are storage tanks covered by provincial pressure equipment law?
faqs.a: No. Atmospheric tanks are not pressure equipment, so they sit outside the provincial pressure equipment regimes. Their programmes rest on fire codes, environmental approvals and API 653, and tanks owned by federally regulated pipeline companies fall under the company's Canada Energy Regulator management system. API 653's RBI-based alternative internal interval is the usual route to risk-based tank intervals.

faqs.q: Does a Canadian RBI study need anyone from Atlantis on site?
faqs.a: No. The study needs no travel: it is delivered remotely from your documents, inspection history and video workshops. Site walkdowns and data verification are done by your own inspectors or your inspection contractor, and where a data gap matters the report specifies the measurement, method and coverage needed so it can be collected locally.

faqs.q: Which RBI methodology do Canadian regulators expect?
faqs.a: Regulators look for a documented, systematic method rather than a particular brand of analysis. API RP 580 and API RP 581 are widely used, ASME PCC-3 is another recognised framework, and many owners have a corporate RBI standard built on one of them. We work to whichever your integrity management system names and show how each interval follows from it.

faqs.q: How do workshops work across time zones?
faqs.a: Workshops are scheduled in the plant's own working hours, whether that is Mountain time in Alberta, Eastern time in Ontario or Atlantic time in New Brunswick. Between sessions the study team continues document review, so actions raised in one workshop are ready for the next.

The person the provincial system recognises: an in-service pressure equipment inspector in Alberta, a TSSA or insurer inspector or the owner-user's certified staff in Ontario, or the authority another province names. The study proposes intervals and tasks with their basis; it does not approve them, and fitness-for-service decisions stay with the owner's engineer.
